messages.subject_clean: semTools: EFA with FIML
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,

I don't really know whether this belongs here - because it's specific to semTools - but I guess if there's an answer to be found, I will find it here. I'm trying to run an EFA with the efaUnrotate function and want to use FIML for missing data handling. Here's some data-generating code:

library(semTools)

set.seed(593720)
tau1 <- rnorm(500,0,1)
tau2 <- rnorm(500,0,1)

lam <- c(.8,.7,.8,.7,.8)

x <- tau1%*%t(lam) + rnorm(2500,0,.1)
y <- tau2%*%t(lam) + rnorm(2500,0,.1)

dat <- data.frame(x,y)
names(dat) <- as.vector(t(outer(c('x','y'),1:5,paste,sep='')))

miss <- matrix(ncol=10,nrow=500,data=sample(c(FALSE,TRUE),5000,c(.9,.1),replace=TRUE))
dat[miss] <- NA

Now, running normal cfa() with FIML is no problem:

mod1 <- '
tau1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5
tau2 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5'

cfa.fiml <- cfa(mod1,dat,missing='fiml')
cfa.fiml

and neither is running the efaUnrotate() with listwise deletion

efa.listwise <- efaUnrotate(dat,2)
efa.listwise

but when I try to run

efa.fiml <- efaUnrotate(dat,2,missing='fiml')

I get

Error in optim(start, FAfn, FAgr, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = lower,  :
  L-BFGS-B needs finite values of 'fn'
In addition: Warning message:
In log(e) : NaNs produced

Any ideas or suggestions what I can do to obtain an EFA with FIML estimation? Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Best, Martin

messages.subject: MANOVA using lavaan
messages.subject_clean: MANOVA using lavaan
messages.body_plain:
I was intrigued by a paper by Finch & French (2013, http://digitalcommons.wayne.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1772&context=jmasm) in which the authors reported very good results for MANOVA under heterogeneity of variance using an SEM.  I am not particularly well versed in SEM or lavaan (yet), but it does seem to be an intuitively reasonable approach to use!

I put together a simple simulation (attached), basing the SEM implementation on a generous post by Terrence Jorgensen (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/PhAAAqYcRGo).  (Warning: the sim takes a while to run, if you do tinker with it you might want to turn the number of iterations down or omit some conditions at first).

Note that this mini-sim only does equal covariance conditions with samples drawn from a multivariate normal distribution, therefore it should behave fairly well.

The Type I error rates using SEM are very high for small samples, which seems reasonable to me given what I do know about SEM + small N, but this was not reported by Finch & French (2013) who used 10/10/10 as their smallest sample size. T1 Error rates are pretty good for 60/60/60.

While I try to work out what the differences are I thought I would go straight to the source and ask the group whether anything obvious stands out to those who have more expertise in this area!

Type I Error Rates

[1,] 1000       1   0.4 2 2 10 0.051   0.051  0.051 0.051 0.119

messages.body_plain:
>
> Is there a way to use the cfa function with FIML and binary variables at the same time?

Specifying missing = "fiml" (FIML stands for "full-information maximum likelihood") is implying that you want to use maximum likelihood estimation, not WLSMV.  There is no analog for FIML when using weighted least squares.  If your data had several ordered categories (at least 5), it might be feasible to simply treat them as continuous and adjust for non-normality using the MLR estimator, but I do not think it would appropriate to do so for binary data.  Your best option would be to use multiple imputation instead.  There is a function in the semTools package that automates the imputation, analysis, and combination of parameters and SEs.

install.packages("semTools")
library(semTools)
?cfa.mi

Terry

>         The Type I error rates using SEM are very high for small
>         samples, which seems reasonable to me given what I do know about
>         SEM + small N,

As it happens, one of my students is looking into this problem as we
speak. The problem in SEM is that all test statistics are "large-sample"
test statistics (LRT, Wald, score). In some settings, we can do better,
and use exact tests and/or use small-sample corrections.

We are looking at ways to do this (so that it works in most settings),
and this will turn SEM into a nice alternative for MANOVA, without its
limitations.

If all goes well, this should go in 0.5-18. Stay tuned.

Yves.

>  From what I have read, chi-sq does over-reject at very small sample
> sizes, so I agree with your intuition.  Given that these are
> multinormally distributed data, I am curious whether the unadjusted ML
> chi-sq would yield better Type I error rates than the Satorra-Bentler
> scaled chi-sq p-value you are currently saving.  I haven't read enough
> about Satorra-Bentler adjustment to know whether it is benign when there
> is no adjustment needed, or whether there is some kind of unintended
> "overadjustment" happening.

In theory, it is benign in the sense that if you have perfect normal
data, the scaling factor should be one exactly, and there will be no
adjustment. However, a sample of N=10 will never look like perfectly
normal data, and this may indeed harm the results.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: multigroup analysis on regression estimates
messages.subject_clean: multigroup analysis on regression estimates
messages.body_plain:
> without any problems. But I was wondering if it's possible now to
> compare the regressions of both models? Can I conclude there is a
> significant difference between the standardized regression estimates?

Hm. That is not trivial. To formally compare unstandardized regression
estimates across groups, you could label them, as in

y ~ c(a1,a2,a3)*x

(where I have assumed there are 3 groups), and then define new
parameters which reflect the difference between two regression coefficients:

diff.a1a2 := a1 - a2
diff.a1a3 := a1 - a3

This would then give you a standard error and a p-value. However, to do
this for standardized regression coefficients, you would need to first
manually compute the standardized regression coefficients. Now, a
standardized beta (z.beta) is simply

z.beta = beta * (sd(x)/sd(y))

You could get the values for the variances of y and x from the diagonal
of inspect(fit, "cov.ov") if they are observed, and inspect(fit,
"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") if they are latent. Suppose the (fitted) variances for y and x
are 10 and 7 in group 1, then you could write

z.a1 = a1 * sqrt(7)/sqrt(10).

The same for z.a2 and z.a2 (but now using the variances of y and x from
groups 2 and 3). And then, finally, you can write

diff.za1za2 := z.a1 - z.a2

> Could it be that the function measurementInvariance() does not work anymore?

The measurementInvariance() function has moved to the semTools package.

> I had to do it this way:
>
> #Model1: configural invariance
>  > fit1 <-sem(model=Model18, data=mydata, estimator="ML", group="V4")
>  >
>  > #Model2: weak invariance
>  > fit2 <-sem(model=Model18, data=mydata, estimator="MLR", group="V4",
> +            group.equal="loadings")
>  >
>  > #Model3: strong invariance
>  > fit3 <-sem(model=Model18, data=mydata, estimator="MLR", group="V4",
> +            group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))
>  > anova(fit1, fit2)

But this is the 'good' way: you see what your are doing.

Yves.

messages.subject: simsem and semTools updates
messages.subject_clean: simsem and semTools updates
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

After having many problems in updating simsem and semTools packages to CRAN for a long time, finally we can update these packages on CRAN. Here are the details of the updates:

[October 2, 2014] Latest Update: semTools, Version 0.4-6

This version is available in CRAN and KRAN. Many new features were introduced in this version.
The quark function is designed to implement the principal component method to reduce the number of auxiliary variables in missing data handling.
Effect size measures for partial invariance are added in the partialInvariance and partialInvarianceCat functions. The details of effect size measures can be found by typing vignette("partialInvariance")
reliability can find the reliability for categorical indicators using Green and Yang's (2009) method.
The maximalRelia function is designed to find maximal reliability of a composite score.
The mvrnonnorm function is designed to have similar feature to the mvrnorm function in MASS package but creates nonnormal distribution. This is simply a short cut to the simulateData in lavaan package when users have population means and covariance in a matrix format.
Bug fixes for auxiliary and NET.

[October 3, 2014] Latest Update: simsem, Version 0.5-8

This version is available on CRAN and KRAN. This version is a maintenance version that fix minor bugs and update codes according to the CRAN policy. The additional feature in this version is that the generate argument in the sim function can take a function. The function must take sample size as its argument and return data frame with appropriate variable names.

Links:
simsem: http://simsem.org/
semTools: https://github.com/simsem/semTools/wiki

Best,
Sunthud

messages.subject: Counting degrees of freedom
messages.subject_clean: Counting degrees of freedom
messages.body_plain:
All,

I have an example below where two models differ by one parameter, but their reported difference in degrees of freedom is 10.  I observed it in both 0.5-16 and 0.5-17.

I thought that I could fix the problem using fixed.x=TRUE, but this doesn't seem to help.  I'm not sure whether this is expected behavior... the first model seems to be counting intercept parameters, while the second model is not.

library(lavaan)

hs39 <- HolzingerSwineford1939
hs39$sch <- as.numeric(hs39$school == "Pasteur")
hsm1     <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              visual ~ sch '

hsm2    <-  ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              visual ~ 0*1 '

fit <- sem(hsm1, data=hs39, meanstructure=TRUE, fixed.x=TRUE)
fit2 <- sem(hsm2, data=hs39, meanstructure=TRUE, fixed.x=TRUE)

## Differ by 10 degrees of freedom
anova(fit, fit2)

## But only one parameter difference
length(coef(fit))
length(coef(fit2))

Of course, the anova command correctly assesses the df difference if hsm2 contains the line

visual ~ 0*sch

Best,
Ed

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ed,

Let me give my two cents. Let's rewrite hsm1 so that all covariances among latent variables are defined:

hsm3     <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              visual ~ sch

 visual ~~ textual
 visual ~~ speed
 textual ~~ speed'

I think that hsm2 is equivalent to the following model:

hsm4    <-  ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9

 x2 + x3 + x5 + x6 + x8 + x9 ~ sch
 visual + textual + speed ~ sch
 visual ~~ textual
 visual ~~ speed
 textual ~~ speed
            '
fit3 <- sem(hsm3, data=hs39, meanstructure=TRUE, fixed.x=TRUE)
fit4 <- sem(hsm4, data=hs39, meanstructure=TRUE, fixed.x=TRUE)

That is the directional relationship from sch to variables in the models are saturated. Then,

anova(fit3, fit2)
anova(fit3, fit4)

will provide the same df differences of 8. Let's go back to hsm1. hsm1 is equivalent to the following model:

hsm5     <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              visual ~ sch

 visual ~~ 0*textual
 visual ~~ 0*speed
 textual ~~ speed'
fit5 <- sem(hsm5, data=hs39, meanstructure=TRUE, fixed.x=TRUE)

Because the residual variances involving visual are fixed as 0, comparing with hsm2 or hsm4 would provide df of 10.

anova(fit5, fit2)
anova(fit5, fit4)
anova(fit, fit2)

messages.body_plain:
On 10/06/2014 09:50 PM, Ed Merkle wrote:
> All,
>
> I have an example below where two models differ by one parameter, but
> their reported difference in degrees of freedom is 10.

The two models are not nested: the two models are based on a different
set of observed variables.

The first model has 10 observed variables (including 'sch'), and
therefore, the number of sample statistics is 10*11/2 + 10 = 65. But
since 'sch' is exogenous, we do not need to count its variance and mean,
so we only have 63 sample statistics. And we have 29 free parameters
(again, we do not count the mean + variance of 'sch'), giving 34 df. (If
we would use fixed.x = FALSE, we would have 65 sample statistics, 31
free parameters, and 34 df).

BTW, 0.5-17 contains the low-level functions lav_partable_ndat(),
lav_partable_npar() and lav_partable_df() to compute these numbers, as in

lav_partable_ndat(parTable(fit))

The second model has only 9 observed variables, and no exogenous
variables. Now, we have 9*10/2 + 9 = 54 sample statistics. And 30 free
parameters, giving 24 df.

The only way out (as Sunthud suggested) is to include 'sch' in both
models, but somehow neutralize its effect in the second model.

In any case, it seems that anova() should give a warning if a different
set of observed variables is used; this is now done in dev 0.5-18.732.

Yves.

ANOVA and friends.

messages.subject: Re: calculating the item-score functions based on lavaan output
messages.subject_clean: calculating the item-score functions based on lavaan output
messages.body_plain:
The logit transformation takes a probability (p) and transforms it using

logit = log( p / (1 - p) )

The equation you are using to transform logits into probabilities is simply the inverse logit function:

p = exp(logit) / (1 + exp(logit))

The probit function, however, takes a probability and finds the associated z score (quantile in a standard normal distribution).  For instance, the z scores associated with -1.96, -1, and 0 should look familiar if you run this syntax:

?qnorm
qnorm(p = c(-1.96, -1, 0))

To transform the probits back into probabilities, you can apply the inverse of the qnorm() function, which is the pnorm() function:

prob <- pnorm(probits)

where I *think* you still use the same equation for calculating an individual's probit from the item and person parameters:

probits <- loading * (trait - threshold)
prob <- pnorm(probits)

These functions are vectorized in R, so you shouldn't have to loop over [i] individuals, but your answer will be the same if you do.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hi

Why are you using lavaan for this? If you just want to predict one observed variable linearly from others, a more simple alternative would be to just use a linear regression model for prediction.

I do not think that lavaan can do predictions directly and your model does not include paths from the predictors to the criterion. What you can do is to get the model implied covariance matrix from Lavaan and then solve the prediction equation from there. Like this: (I have not tested this code)

fit <- sem(YOUR MODEL AND DATA)

i <- INDEX OF PREDICTED VARIABLE
j <- INDICES OF PREDICTOR VARIABLES

cv <- fitted(fit)$cov
coef <- solve(cv[j,j],cv[j,i])

predictions <- YOUR_DATA[,j]%*% coef

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I cannot really give you any exact references for full approach, but this is based on two principles

1) The model implied covariance matrix is maximum likelihood estimate of the population covariance matrix given the model structure

2) If you have a covariance matrix, then OLS regression gives optimal linear predictions.

You can find these two facts in any decent SEM and regression textbooks. My favorites that I would cite are

Bollen, K. A. (1989). Structural Equations with Latent Variables. New York, NY: John Wiley & Son Inc.
Wooldridge, J. M. (2009). Introductory econometrics: a modern approach (4th ed.). Mason, OH: South Western, Cengage Learning.

messages.subject_clean: zero.cell.warn - when are empty cells in a bivariate table an issue?
messages.body_plain:
On 10/09/2014 09:38 PM, Michael Paul Grosz wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I noticed that since I use the new lavaan version ( version 0.5-17) , I
> get many warnings regarding empty cells in the bivariate tables.

> (When) do I need to be concerned about such warnings? and what are remedies?

It depends. They are warnings, not errors. But it doesn't hurt to have a
look at some of these bivariate frequency tables. You can use the
lavTables() function for that. (or you can use use table() with two of
your variables)

If only one or two cells (out of 36) are empty, that is probably nothing
to worry about. But if you have many empty cells in a single table, it
gets harder to estimate the polychoric correlation for that table.

In that case, you can either treat the data as continuous (for 6-point
likert scales, this may be a reasonable approach), or collapse some
categories, and create, say 4-point scales for some or all the items.

Yves.

messages.subject: Residuals of a latent regression to predict further variables / higher order factor identification
messages.subject_clean: Residuals of a latent regression to predict further variables / higher order factor identification
messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan fellows,

I want to use the residuals of a latent regression to predict a third variable, that is:

- Variable 1 predicts Variable 2
- Residuals of Variable 2 (i.e., withouth the influence of Variable 1) and Variable 1 predict Variable 3

It is sometimes used in the literature, for example in Wüstenberg et al. (2012), page 9-10, Figure 5 (see attachment). They used a MPlus syntax like this one:

F1 by ind11 ind12 ind13;
F2 by ind21 ind22 ind23;
F3 by ind31 ind32 ind33;

F2 on F1;
F2_residual by F2;
F2@0;
F2_residual with F1@0;

F3 on F2_residual F1;

I would adapt it to lavaan in this way:

F1 =~ ind11 ind12 ind13
F2 =~ ind21 ind22 ind23
F3 =~ ind31 ind32 ind33

F2 ~ F1
F2_residual =~ F2
F2 ~~ 0*F2
F2_residual ~~ 0*F1

F3 ~ F2_residual F1

Would you agree?

Well, actually my Factor 2 is a higher order factor of two latent factors. According to Brown (2006), page 205, Figure 5.3, and some thoughts about identification I would model Factor 2 in this way:

F2.1 =~ NA*ind21 ind22 ind23
F2.2 =~ NA*ind24 ind25 ind26
F2.1 ~~ 1*F2.1
F2.2 ~~ 1*F2.2

F2 =~ NA*F2.1 + a*F2.1 + a*F2.2
F2 ~~ 1*F2

That is, the factor loadings of the latent factors to the higher order factor are constrained to equality for identification issues. Still okay?

Okay, now there is a problem with the combined syntax:

# measurement models
F2.1 =~ NA*ind21 ind22 ind23
F2.2 =~ NA*ind24 ind25 ind26
F2.1 ~~ 1*F2.1
F2.2 ~~ 1*F2.2
F2 =~ NA*F2.1 + a*F2.1 + a*F2.2
F2 ~~ 1*F2

F1 =~ ind11 ind12 ind13
F3 =~ ind31 ind32 ind33

# structural models
F2 ~ F1
F2_residual =~ F2
F2 ~~ 0*F2
F2_residual ~~ 0*F1

F3 ~ F2_residual F1

It produces this error message:

> Error in lavParseModelString(model) :
>   lavaan ERROR: duplicate model element in: F2~~0*F2

I understand the problem (F2 ~~1*F2 vs F2~~0*F2) somehow, but I do not know a solution. Is there another possibilty to model Factor 2 in a way that I can skip F2 ~~1*F2? Or is there another way to use the residuals of Factor 2?

Best,
André

References:
Brown, T. A. (2006). Confirmatory factor analysis for applied research. New York: Guilford Press.
Wüstenberg, S., Greiff, S., & Funke, J. (2012). Complex problem solving — More than reasoning? Intelligence, 40, 1–14. doi:10.1016/j.intell.2011.11.003

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ed,

When using summary, there's only one slot for a chi-square so that's all we report (the Mplus chi-square in that case. To see all the chi-square values try using inspect(fit, "impute").

One note on the output. The results from the ML and LMRR fit statistics are F statistics. To convert to a chi-square, multiply the F value by the model df.

Alex

P. S. I'm very aware of the issues surrounding missing data in any number of fields. A perceived barrier to modern methods of handling missing data is that they are perceived to be too "hard" for many applied researchers to learn. One of our goals with runMI was to provide a straightforward implementation of MI using SEM. The more tools like this we have the better adoption will be (I hope!).

messages.body_plain:
The “BY” syntax in the Mplus codes implies a higher order factor, but I think that is a mistake.  You do have to fix its variance and force it to be orthogonal to F1, but I think your task is simpler than this, as long as you directly fix the parameters that need fixing.

F1 =~ ind11 + ind12 + ind13
F2 =~ ind21 + ind22 + ind23
F3 =~ ind31 + ind32 + ind33

F2 ~ F1 + F2_residual
F2 ~~ 0*F2
F2_residual ~~ 1*F2_residual

F2_residual ~~ 0*F1

F3 ~ F2_residual + F1

I would expect this to work.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Re: How to do predictions on lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: How to do predictions on lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
That's not exactly what the SEM in your diagram represents.  The indicators are not predictors of satisfaction.  The indicators are outcomes of the latent variables (just like the satisfaction is an outcome of the latent variables).  In principle, your model is equivalent to one in which satisfaction is a multidimensional indicator of the latent constructs, whereas the other indicators are unidimensional indicators of only one construct each (but that is obviously not representative of your theory).

Hypothetically, if only ONE of your indicators changed its level while the other indicators of the same construct remained at the same levels, then the cause of that change would be due to something unique about that indicator, not common to all the indicators.  The latent variable represents the source of the common variance among all the indicators.  If you think there is something unique about an indicator that is predictive of satisfaction (beyond what the latent construct itself explains about satisfaction), then you need a regression path from that indicator to satisfaction, or equivalently, another latent variable that is pointing to both that indicator and to satisfaction.

If, however, you want to see how the predicted values of satisfaction would change as levels of the predictor(s) (i.e., the latent variables) change, then you already have the information you need in the lavaan output.  Save the regression coefficients, then create a new data object (the way you would to use the predict method for an lm or glm object) that contains combinations of values of your latent variables, then plug those "newdata" values into the regression equation to generate predicted values.

For example, if you have 2 latent variables (L1 and L2), then your regression coefficients can be found in the "Intercepts" and "Regressions" sections of the summary() output from the lavaan object.  Save those values as b0, b1, and b2.  If you used the fixed-factor method of identification, then you can pick 3 meaningful levels of the latent variable: the mean (0) and 1 SD above and below the mean (+/- 1).  Put all combinations of these into a single data frame:

newdata <- expand.grid(L1 = c(-1, 0, 1), L2 = -1:1)
newdata

Then calculate predicted values by plugging them into the regression equation:

newdata$pred <- b0 + b1*newdata$L1 + b2*newdata$L2
newdata

Finally, you can plot the predicted values

plot(pred ~ L1, data = newdata[newdata$L2 == 0, ], type = "l")
plot(pred ~ L2, data = newdata[newdata$L1 == 1, ], type = "l")

If you want to get fancy, there is a 3D plot in the "rgl" package, that the "car" package capitalizes on:

install.packages(c("car", "rgl"))
library(car)
scatter3d(pred ~ L1 + L2, data = newdata, fit = "smooth")

messages.body_plain:
A second order model with three first order factors is equivalent to a model with three correlated factors.  With only 2 first order factors, some additional constraint must be imposed to make the second order model statistically identified.  Once that is done, though, you again achieve equivalence between the two approaches.  It may be that the ordered nature of your observed variables is inducing that additional constraint.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ni Wi--
     In factor-based SEM, estimation is generally simultaneous.  All of the predictors of each dependent variable are gathered together in one equation--as with regression with one dependent.  As in such a regression, if you have two correlated predictors, the variance in the dependent which they jointly predict is not credited to either predictor, though it is counted as explained by both predictors together.  Factor structures generally minimize this problem as a side effect of identification constraints.  Models with the same observed variables loading on multiple factors typically impose orthogonality constraints on the multiple factors, solving both problems at once.
--Ed Rigdon

On 10/15/2014 09:40 PM, in...@vbi.vt.edu wrote:
> Hi Yves,
>    I am fitting the following model in lavaan (this is not a very
> interesting model, it just arises in a series of models and gives me an
> error):
>
> SNP.gex.meth.cor <- '
>      meth ~ 1   +  methSNP1
>      gex ~ 1
>      meth ~~ meth
>      gex ~~ gex
>      meth ~~ gex
> '

This looks like a bug in lavaan. lavaan 'thinks' this is a univariate
regression model:

lavaan (0.5-18.733) converged normally after   1 iterations

and calls lm.fit() (instead of the lavaan engine) to get the parameters.
Only, this is isn't just a univariate regression. One way around this is
as follows:

SNP.gex.meth.cor <- '
     meth ~ 1   +  methSNP1

     gex ~ 1 + 0*methSNP1

     meth ~~ meth
     gex ~~ gex
     meth ~~ gex
'

now lavaan will see two regressions, and use the lavaan engine (instead
of lm), and everything will be fine.

The lesson for me is that univariate regressions are hard to spot.

Yves.

בתאריך יום רביעי, 15 באוקטובר 2014 16:58:45 UTC+3, מאת Edward Rigdon:

> Dear Ni Wi--
>      In factor-based SEM, estimation is generally simultaneous.  All of the predictors of each dependent variable are gathered together in one equation--as with regression with one dependent.  As in such a regression, if you have two correlated predictors, the variance in the dependent which they jointly predict is not credited to either predictor, though it is counted as explained by both predictors together.  Factor structures generally minimize this problem as a side effect of identification constraints.  Models with the same observed variables loading on multiple factors typically impose orthogonality constraints on the multiple factors, solving both problems at once.
> --Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Re: hybrid multidimensional CFA model: a second order construct with first-order formative dimensions
messages.subject_clean: hybrid multidimensional CFA model: a second order construct with first-order formative dimensions
messages.body_plain:
Hi

The formative part is not identified. You always need reflective variables to identify the model, or alternatively you need to fix the formative paths to know values.

This should be identified:

IPFpasswork =~ X1pw + X2pw + X3pw + X4pw
IDpasswork =~ IDwork

IDwork ~~ 0* IDwork

IPFentrpass =~ X1ep + X2ep + X3ep
IDentrpass =~ IDdev

IDdev ~~ 0*IDdev

Passforwork<~ 1*IPFpasswork + 1*IDpasswork
Entrpass<~ 1*IPFentrpass + 1*IDentrpass

There was a similar question on the SEMNET just today or yesterday, and you might want to search the archives on that mailing list for the responses.

Mikko

> On 21 Oct 2014, at 18:52 , Sunthud Pornprasertmanit <psun...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> You have factors that have only one indicator. I recommend you to avoid using latent variables for single indicators. For example,
>
> Independentmodel <-'
> IPFpasswork =~ X1pw + X2pw + X3pw + X4pw
> IPFentrpass =~ X1ep + X2ep + X3ep
> Passforwork<~ IPFpasswork + IDwork
> Entrpass<~ IPFentrpass * IDdev
> '
> fit<-cfa(Independentmodel, data = Passwork.and.entrpass)
>
> P.S. I am not good on the formative factors. I am not sure whether this script is still non-identified.
>

messages.subject: Re: MIMIC model with 3 composite/formative variables
messages.subject_clean: MIMIC model with 3 composite/formative variables
messages.body_plain:
See Kline (2011), "Another way to remedy identification problems is to add effect indicators for latent composites represented in the original model as measured with cause indicators only. That is, specify a MIMIC factor. For example, adding two effect indicators means that the formerly latent composite will emit at least two direct effects---see Diamantopoulos, Riefler, and Roth (2008) for examples" (p. 283). I've attached Diamantopoulos et al (2008), see section 5.3.3.1. See also Acock (2013), Chapter 3.5.2 Multiple indicators, multiple causes model. See also Mplus Topic 1 slides, slide 244 model 4. These kinds of models are what I'm trying to specify. Based on your answer can I assume there's no option for this in lavaan?

messages.subject: Re: Model is not identified & No Standard Errors computed!!!
messages.subject_clean: Model is not identified & No Standard Errors computed!!!
messages.body_plain:
Hi

The model is not identified because you have single indicator LVs. You need to fix the error terms (e.g to zero or a value taken from existing research.)

pis1=~Views_2009
Views_2009~~0*Views_2009

Your model seems to be longitudinal, in which case things get a bit more complicated when you think how to fix the parameter values because you need to consider measurement invariance. I recommend the boo by Todd Little on the topic.

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: MIMIC model with 3 composite/formative variables
messages.subject_clean: MIMIC model with 3 composite/formative variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi

There is no need for the conceptual difference between formative and reflective indicators. But if you add two reflective indicators, then the model is identified just with those indicators and there is no need for the formative part. In fact, there is no apparent advantage in including the formative part at all if you have reflective indicators. Additionally, unless the assumption of no measurement error in the formative indicators hold exactly, your results will be biased if you include the formative indicators.

We address this in a recent paper

Rönkkö, M., & Aguirre-Urreta, M. I. (2014). Formative Measurement when Indicators Contain Error: Analysis of Ten Alternative Approaches. In Academy of Management Best Papers Proceedings.

I can send the paper off list or you can get it from the AoM conference website.

Mikko

> On 21 Oct 2014, at 19:21 , Amanda Pollitt <ampoll...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> See Kline (2011), "Another way to remedy identification problems is to add effect indicators for latent composites represented in the original model as measured with cause indicators only. That is, specify a MIMIC factor. For example, adding two effect indicators means that the formerly latent composite will emit at least two direct effects---see Diamantopoulos, Riefler, and Roth (2008) for examples" (p. 283). I've attached Diamantopoulos et al (2008), see section 5.3.3.1. See also Acock (2013), Chapter 3.5.2 Multiple indicators, multiple causes model. See also Mplus Topic 1 slides, slide 244 model 4. These kinds of models are what I'm trying to specify. Based on your answer can I assume there's no option for this in lavaan?
>

> >
> > conceptually, this does not make sense: latent variables are either

> >
> > Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I would recommend starting by estimating small parts of the model. When you add parts to the model one at a time, then you know which part is problematic and can identify the problem better.

Mikko

messages.subject_clean: MIMIC model with 3 composite/formative variables
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the information, this is a useful paper. However, theoretically my model requires formative indicators. They are measures of financial stress, similar to SES (but not exactly). The causal indicators are financial strain (do you receive food stamps?), financial access (do you own a car or truck?), and income. The effect indicators are health variables which would not theoretically form a construct of financial stress but financial stress does predict health.

On Tuesday, October 21, 2014 9:30:19 AM UTC-7, Mikko Rönkkö wrote:
> Hi
>
> There is no need for the conceptual difference between formative and reflective indicators. But if you add two reflective indicators, then the model is identified just with those indicators and there is no need for the formative part. In fact, there is no apparent advantage in including the formative part at all if you have reflective indicators. Additionally, unless the assumption of no measurement error in the formative indicators hold exactly, your results will be biased if you include the formative indicators.
>
> We address this in a recent paper
>
> Rönkkö, M., & Aguirre-Urreta, M. I. (2014). Formative Measurement when Indicators Contain Error: Analysis of Ten Alternative Approaches. In Academy of Management Best Papers Proceedings.
>
>
> I can send the paper off list or you can get it from the AoM conference website.
>
> Mikko
>
> > On 21 Oct 2014, at 19:21 , Amanda Pollitt <ampoll...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > See Kline (2011), "Another way to remedy identification problems is to add effect indicators for latent composites represented in the original model as measured with cause indicators only. That is, specify a MIMIC factor. For example, adding two effect indicators means that the formerly latent composite will emit at least two direct effects---see Diamantopoulos, Riefler, and Roth (2008) for examples" (p. 283). I've attached Diamantopoulos et al (2008), see section 5.3.3.1. See also Acock (2013), Chapter 3.5.2 Multiple indicators, multiple causes model. See also Mplus Topic 1 slides, slide 244 model 4. These kinds of models are what I'm trying to specify. Based on your answer can I assume there's no option for this in lavaan?
> >
> > On Monday, October 20, 2014 11:24:57 PM UTC-7, yrosseel wrote:
> > > On 10/20/2014 11:03 PM, Amanda Pollitt wrote:
> > > > pfinstress <~ 1*pa56 + pa57c + pa57d + pa57f
> > > > pfinstress =~ pa20 + pa58
> > >
> > > conceptually, this does not make sense: latent variables are either
> > > formative or reflective.
> > >
> > > Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Hi

> On 21 Oct 2014, at 19:53 , Amanda Pollitt <ampoll...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you for the information, this is a useful paper. However, theoretically my model requires formative indicators. They are measures of financial stress, similar to SES (but not exactly). The causal indicators are financial strain (do you receive food stamps?), financial access (do you own a car or truck?), and income. The effect indicators are health variables which would not theoretically form a construct of financial stress but financial stress does predict health.

If you have valid reflective and formative indicators for your construct, it would be correct to say that the construct can be measured either reflectively or formatively or with both modes of measurement at the same time, right?

If your construct cannot be measured reflectively, then you cannot add the two reflective indicators because that would result in an invalid model. In this case your only option would be to fix all parameters of the formative model to known values because they cannot be estimated because of lack of identification.

So the question is, do you have valid reflective indicators? If you do, then simply using those is enough to identify the model; you would have two overlapping measurement systems and not both are required.

messages.subject: Re: MIMIC model with 3 composite/formative variables
messages.subject_clean: MIMIC model with 3 composite/formative variables
messages.body_plain:
The purpose of a MIMIC model is to allow for estimation of the measurement error of the composite construct. Acock's (2013) example was of child learning environment. He used causal indicators of mother's education, family income, number of siblings, parental support, and parental monitoring and effect indicators of academic achievement, level of educational aspirations, and level of the teacher's ratings. According to Acock, this allows estimation of the error variance of the composite latent variable so we no longer have to assume that there is no measurement error, thus avoiding the bias you discuss. (p. 146)

Like SES, a theoretically correct measurement model of financial stress cannot be made using effect indicators.

Is there code for specifying MIMIC models in lavaan?

On 10/22/2014 01:47 AM, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> Amanda--

> get an R2 just as well that way.

Agreed. In my original reply (see below), I wrote 'conceptually'.
Perhaps I should have written 'Syntactically'.

>>>>             On 10/20/2014 11:03 PM, Amanda Pollitt wrote:
>>>>             > pfinstress <~ 1*pa56 + pa57c + pa57d + pa57f
>>>>             > pfinstress =~ pa20 + pa58
>>>>
>>>>             conceptually, this does not make sense: latent variables
>>>>             are either
>>>>             formative or reflective.
>>>>
>>>>             Yves.

What I wanted to point out is that

pfinstress <~ x1 + x2 + x3

is just syntax sugar for this:

pfinstress =~ 0
pfinstress ~~ 0*pfinstress
pfinstress ~ x1 + x2 + x3

and you can write

pfinstress <~ 1*pa56 + pa57c + pa57d + pa57f
pfinstress =~ pa20 + pa58

as

pfinstress =~ pa20 + pa58
pfinstress ~ 1*pa56 + pa57c + pa57d + pa57f

# pfinstress ~~ 0*pfinstress

where -depending on your view- you can allow the (residual) variance of
'pfinstress' to be zero or not.

Yves.

Hi Conal,

If this is the case, then your syntax included above doesn't have that information. You specified two factors measured at a single timepoint. For a two factor scale measured twice there should be 4 factors (Factor 1 Time 1, Factor 2 Time 1, Factor 1 Time 2, and Factor 2 Time 2). In addition (Sunthud can probably confirm this), I think the longInvariance function only works for a single factor measured multiple times, not multiple factors at multiple times. In your case you might have to specify the invariance models "by hand."

Alex

messages.subject: multiple group SEM with dummy variables that are zero for certain groups
messages.subject_clean: multiple group SEM with dummy variables that are zero for certain groups
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am wondering if it is possible to fit a multiple group SEM in which categorical variables are coded as dummies, some of which only have zeroes in a certain group.
Let's say we have a SEM that look like this:

model <- '
# regressions
        y1 ~  x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
        y2 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
        y3  ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
        y4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
        y5 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
        y6 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5
# residual covariances
        y1 ~~ y2
        y1 ~~ y3
        y1 ~~ y4
        y2 ~~ y3
        y2 ~~ y4
        y3 ~~ y4
        '
fit <- sem(model, data=data, group = "group")

With group having 2 levels. A model like that runs just fine. Now suppose these data come from 6 plots, 3 of wich were located in group 1 (plot 1, plot 3, plot 5) and 3 of which were located in group 2 (plot 2, plot 4, plot 6). One could then construct 5 dummy variables, plot2, plot3, plot4, plot5, plot6.

The problem is that in any of the models below, for group 1 the variables plot2, plot4 and plot6 consist entirely of zeroes, as do plot3 and plot5 for group 2. If I try to run anything like that, I get errors. So my question is, is it even possible to fit a model like that? I know the alternative is to split the data per group and run a separate SEM (this works) but then I miss out on the options that come with a multiple group SEM.

This does not work:

model <- '
# regressions
        y1 ~  x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot2 + plot3 + pot4 + plot5 + plot6
        y2 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot2 + plot3 + pot4 + plot5 + plot6
        y3  ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot2 + plot3 + pot4 + plot5 + plot6
        y4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot2 + plot3 + pot4 + plot5 + plot6
        y5 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + plot2 + plot3 + pot4 + plot5 + plot6
        y6 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + plot2 + plot3 + pot4 + plot5 + plot6
# residual covariances
        y1 ~~ y2
        y1 ~~ y3
        y1 ~~ y4
        y2 ~~ y3
        y2 ~~ y4
        y3 ~~ y4
        '
fit <- sem(model, data=data, group = "group")

Neither does this:

model <- '
# composites
        plot <~1*plot2 + plot3 + plot4 + plot5 + plot6
# regressions
        y1 ~  x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot
        y2 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot
        y3  ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot
        y4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot
        y5 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + plot
        y6 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + plot
# residual covariances
        y1 ~~ y2
        y1 ~~ y3
        y1 ~~ y4
        y2 ~~ y3
        y2 ~~ y4
        y3 ~~ y4
        '
fit <- sem(model, data=data, group = "group")

I tried removing "plot2" as well, I tried fixing the parameters to zero for the groups in which these parameters should be zero by specifying for example "c(0,NA)*plot4". Nothing seems to work. This makes me suspect that what I am trying to achieve is not possible, but it would be nice to have this confirmed by someone with a better understanding of these matters.

Any help or insights would be much appreciated,
M.

> Yes, I mean a binary outcome. I tried MML, but it takes literally hours.

You mentioned you did not want to use WLSMV. Why? What about estimator =
"PML" (pairwise ML). Only if you have categorical indicators only (for now).

> Is there any "trick" to do my logistic regressions "outside" the SE
> model in a clever way?

Perhaps. How does your model look like? What do you want to achieve? It
might be possible to compute so-called 'factor scores' for the latent
variables (using either the Bartlett or the regression method, see
Skrondal & Laake, 2001). Next, you can use glm(), and if done right, you
might get unbiased (unstandardized) regression coefficients.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: multiple group SEM with dummy variables that are zero for certain groups
messages.subject_clean: multiple group SEM with dummy variables that are zero for certain groups
messages.body_plain:
> Could you give an example of how to code this in lavaan, perhaps using the example I posted?
>

Interesting -- in ANOVA context, these would be called "nested factors," right?  Within each level of the first grouping variable "group" there are unique levels of the second grouping variable "plot" so the factors cannot be analyzed as fully crossed.  I had a similar experience when I looked at the effect of a certain stimulus on willingness to vote for a 3rd-party candidate.  For Republican participants, the choices were either a Republican or Libertarian candidate, and for Democrat participants, the choices were either a Democrat or Green Party candidate.  Check out Chapter 10 of Maxwell & Delaney (2004) for more details about difficulties in an ANOVA context, which could still be quite informative in the SEM context.

http://books.google.com/books/about/Designing_Experiments_and_Analyzing_Data.html?id=h-bMhmQMifsC

Anyway, I'm not sure if I'm thinking of the same solution as Ed, but I think he's suggesting (and I would agree) to NOT run it as a 2-group model (using the "group" variable for the argument group) with separate dummy codes for levels of plot.  This doesn't work because as you said, each dummy code is a constant (rather than a variable) in one group or the other, so the variance in that group would be zero, resulting in non/semi-positive-definite input matrices.  And you can't simply include one subset of dummy codes for the group-1 model and the other subset for the group-2 model because the same model needs to be fit to the "same" means/covariance matrix in each group.

The solution, I think, is to instead use the "plot" indicator (not dummy codes, but a grouping variable with 6 levels) as the argument to group, so it would be a 6-group model.

> model <- '
> # regressions
>         y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
>         y5 + y6 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
>         y6 ~ y5
> # residual covariances
>         y1 ~~ y2 + y3 + y4
>         y2 ~~ y3 + y4
>         y3 ~~ y4
> '
> fit <- sem(model, data=data, group = "plot")

This is equivalent to including the interaction term in your original syntax (e.g., y1 ~ y2 + plot2 + y2*plot2) because the effect of y2 can be different for each level of plot (equivalently, the mean-differences between plots can vary as a function of y2).  Knowing how the factors are nested, you can simply add constraints if you want to "exclude the interaction term" and test whether that constraint is valid using anova().  Here's an example for just one of your outcomes (y1):

> model <- '
> # regressions
>         y1 ~ c("x1a", "x1b", "x1a", "x1b", "x1a", "x1b")*x1
>         y1 ~ c("x2a", "x2b", "x2a", "x2b", "x2a", "x2b")*x2
>         y1 ~ c("x3a", "x3b", "x3a", "x3b", "x3a", "x3b")*x3
>         y1 ~ c("x4a", "x4b", "x4a", "x4b", "x4a", "x4b")*x4

>         y2 + y3 + y4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
>         y5 + y6 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
>         y6 ~ y5
> # residual covariances
>         y1 ~~ y2 + y3 + y4
>         y2 ~~ y3 + y4
>         y3 ~~ y4
> '

The above syntax constrains the slope for x1 to be the same within group 1 (i.e., plots 1, 3, and 5) and within group 2 (i.e., plots 2, 4, and 6) without forcing groups 1 and 2 to equality.  Likewise for the slopes of x2, x3, and x4.  Similar syntax can be added for the other outcomes, as well.  I'm not sure whether that's a hypothesis you wanted to test, but the basic idea is that you are running a 6-group model, and any constraints you add to compare groups can be applied by equating plots 1, 3, and 5, as well as plots 2, 4, and 6.  This respects the nested structure of your factors.

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Experimental Design with SEM analysis
messages.body_plain:
> For example, I have three manipulated groups; Low, Moderate, and High.
> First, I code their values as 1 for low, 2 for moderate, and 3 for high; it becomes 3 point likert type of scale.

This is an ordered grouping variable with very few categories.  The coding (1,2,3) is fine, but I would not treat it as though it were continuous.  For example, if you insist on entering it as an exogenous predictor in your model, it would be preferable to create 2 dummy codes.

But I think it would be better to use the grouping variable (coded [1,2,3], not as 2 dummy codes) to run a 3-group model.  This relaxes the assumption of homoscedasticity across experimental conditions because each group will have its own residual variance parameter, rather than a single common residual variance if you use the dummy codes as you would in a typical regression/ANCOVA model.  Relaxing this assumption is a big advantage of SEM over the general linear model.

> Third, I also model some other exogenous and endogenous variables; these variables are measured by 9 point likert type of scale.

These variables can be treated as continuous predictors, but I would use the MLR estimator to correct for non-normality if the histograms suggest the variables are not approximately normal.

Running this as a multiple-group model implicitly allows for interaction terms unless you constrain parameters to equivalence across groups.  For example, if you your outcome is called Y, predictor is called X, and experimental grouping variable is called G, your script for the multiple-group model would look like this:

> syntax0 <- ' Y ~ X '
> out0 <- sem(syntax0, data = myData, group = "G")

The regression parameter is uniquely estimated in each group, so it is equivalent to running a linear model like this (using the Moderate group as a reference group, and having dummy codes for the Low and High groups):

> lm(Y ~ X + Low + High + Low*X + High*X, data = myData)

If you wanted to test the interactions for significance, you would need to constrain the regression parameters to equality across groups by giving those parameters the same label.

> syntax1 <- ' Y ~ c(b1, b1, b1)*X '
> out1 <- sem(syntax1, data = myData, group = "G")
> ## equivalent to below, but not as flexible if
> ## you just want to compare one pair of groups at a time
> out1 <- sem(syntax0, data = myData, group = "G", group.equal = "regressions")

This is equivalent to a "main"-effects model:

> lm(Y ~ X + Low + High, data = myData)

This is a simple example, but the same principal applies to more complex cases (e.g., multiple outcomes).  If you have latent variables, you'll need to establish measurement invariance before testing latent parameters.  There are many more details about running multiple-group models on the lavaan tutorials page: http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

Terry

messages.subject: Re: logistic regression in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: logistic regression in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
> (a) Is "logit" available or not? I want to use logistic regression to predict Y.

No, not yet.

> (b) If logit is not availble, I will have to use the default which is probit. Thats fine, but I do not know how to use probit to make various scenarios in lavaan e.g. if x1=xx and x2=xxx and x3=xxxx and x4=xxxxx then the probability for Y=1 is 20%.

There is a plethora of literature showing that logit and probit give nearly identical results.  The difference is merely the link function.  The logit function takes a probability P (bound between 0 and 1) and transforms it to a logit (LO) on an unbounded continuum:

> LO = logit(P) = log( P / (1 - P) )
> P = inverse-logit(LO) = exp(LO) / ( 1 + exp(LO) )
>
The probit function takes the same probability P and puts in on an unbounded continuum by finding the associated Z score in a standard normal distribution, easily calculated in R using the normal distribution functions:

> Z = probit(P) = qnorm(P, mean = 0, sd = 1)
> P = pnorm(Z, mean = 0, sd = 1)

The mean/sd arguments are 0/1 by default, so I just included them for illustration.  As in logistic regression, there is not much point in directly interpreting a probit slope.  In probit regression, the slope represents how many z-scores you expect the "outcome" (the probability the outcome = 1) to change for a single unit-increase in that predictor.  In logistic regression, the slope represents how many logit-units you expect the "outcome" (probability the outcome = 1) to change for a single unit-increase in that predictor.  Of course, in logistic regression, you can exponentiate both sides of the equation, which translates into this interpretation: For a 1-unit increase in the predictor, there is a <exponentiated slope> multiplicative change in the ODDS of the outcome (i.e., the exponentiated slope is an odds ratio).  There is no analogously intuitive interpretation of the probit slopes, but you can generate predicted values of the outcome (in Z scores) for certain levels of the predictor(s), then transform those predicted values into probabilities using the pnorm() function as above. Even if those predictors are latent variables, you can choose representative values on the scale of that variable (e.g., the mean and +/- 1 SD from the mean).  You can find more information in the literature or online, for example:

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/42956/how-do-i-interpret-a-probit-model-in-stata
http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/stata/output/Stata_Probit.htm

Terry

On Sat, Oct 25, 2014 at 1:02 AM, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Could you give an example of how to code this in lavaan, perhaps using the example I posted?
> >
>
> Interesting -- in ANOVA context, these would be called "nested factors," right?  Within each level of the first grouping variable "group" there are unique levels of the second grouping variable "plot" so the factors cannot be analyzed as fully crossed.  I had a similar experience when I looked at the effect of a certain stimulus on willingness to vote for a 3rd-party candidate.  For Republican participants, the choices were either a Republican or Libertarian candidate, and for Democrat participants, the choices were either a Democrat or Green Party candidate.  Check out Chapter 10 of Maxwell & Delaney (2004) for more details about difficulties in an ANOVA context, which could still be quite informative in the SEM context.
>
> http://books.google.com/books/about/Designing_Experiments_and_Analyzing_Data.html?id=h-bMhmQMifsC
>
> Anyway, I'm not sure if I'm thinking of the same solution as Ed, but I think he's suggesting (and I would agree) to NOT run it as a 2-group model (using the "group" variable for the argument group) with separate dummy codes for levels of plot.  This doesn't work because as you said, each dummy code is a constant (rather than a variable) in one group or the other, so the variance in that group would be zero, resulting in non/semi-positive-definite input matrices.  And you can't simply include one subset of dummy codes for the group-1 model and the other subset for the group-2 model because the same model needs to be fit to the "same" means/covariance matrix in each group.
>
> The solution, I think, is to instead use the "plot" indicator (not dummy codes, but a grouping variable with 6 levels) as the argument to group, so it would be a 6-group model.
>
> > model <- '
> > # regressions
> >         y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
> >         y5 + y6 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
> >         y6 ~ y5
> > # residual covariances
> >         y1 ~~ y2 + y3 + y4
> >         y2 ~~ y3 + y4
> >         y3 ~~ y4
> > '
> > fit <- sem(model, data=data, group = "plot")
>
> This is equivalent to including the interaction term in your original syntax (e.g., y1 ~ y2 + plot2 + y2*plot2) because the effect of y2 can be different for each level of plot (equivalently, the mean-differences between plots can vary as a function of y2).  Knowing how the factors are nested, you can simply add constraints if you want to "exclude the interaction term" and test whether that constraint is valid using anova().  Here's an example for just one of your outcomes (y1):
>
> > model <- '
> > # regressions
> >         y1 ~ c("x1a", "x1b", "x1a", "x1b", "x1a", "x1b")*x1
> >         y1 ~ c("x2a", "x2b", "x2a", "x2b", "x2a", "x2b")*x2
> >         y1 ~ c("x3a", "x3b", "x3a", "x3b", "x3a", "x3b")*x3
> >         y1 ~ c("x4a", "x4b", "x4a", "x4b", "x4a", "x4b")*x4
>
> >         y2 + y3 + y4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
> >         y5 + y6 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
> >         y6 ~ y5
> > # residual covariances
> >         y1 ~~ y2 + y3 + y4
> >         y2 ~~ y3 + y4
> >         y3 ~~ y4
> > '
>
> The above syntax constrains the slope for x1 to be the same within group 1 (i.e., plots 1, 3, and 5) and within group 2 (i.e., plots 2, 4, and 6) without forcing groups 1 and 2 to equality.  Likewise for the slopes of x2, x3, and x4.  Similar syntax can be added for the other outcomes, as well.  I'm not sure whether that's a hypothesis you wanted to test, but the basic idea is that you are running a 6-group model, and any constraints you add to compare groups can be applied by equating plots 1, 3, and 5, as well as plots 2, 4, and 6.  This respects the nested structure of your factors.
>
> Terry

messages.subject: effect of demographic variables on chi-square fit
messages.subject_clean: effect of demographic variables on chi-square fit
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
 I have a rather naive question. I searched in many places, but people seem to tend to avoid addressing this issue.

I analyzed some data using lavaan (ofcourse). The model-data fit is excellent even with the strictest criteria like robust chi-square etc. e.g. Robust x2(3)=0.735, p=0.865.
So, this is a great model because it is simple and pseudo-R squared =0.39. Two latent factors predict a binary dependent variable.

This is the interesting part: However, when I add in the binary regression part of the model another predictor e.g. gender, then the model of the fit becomes much worse, i.e. robust x2(7)=56.97, p<0.0001. I understand that this is an indication that the inclusion of the demographic variables in the model is not needed and the model "complains". The demographic variable gender is not related to the latent factors of the model, becasue when I check the Modificatio Indices they do not have high values. But the pseudo-R squared increases to 0.42 , so it makes some sense to add the variable in the model.

So my question is: Why does the chi-square increase so much, if the modification indices do not seem to be inflated and if the Rsquared increases (even by a small increase?).

Also: Should I report the model-fit statistics before adding the demographic variable or after? I have noticed that this happened with many of my datasets.  Any ideas?

Thank you for your time

On 10/27/2014 12:46 PM, phitho29 wrote:
> Hi Ed,
>
> thanks for your reply. I'm still confused: My results change dependent
> on the estimator I use. As I understand it, df's should not change when
> switching between ML and MLM estimation? In both cases, I'm using the
> lavaan function. The only thing I'm changing is the estimator (from ML
> to MLM). Why do the df's change?

Because MLM requires a meanstructure, while ML does not. And although
the lavaan() function will add model parameters for the means, they are
-by default- fixed to zero. If you allow them to be free, the df's will
be the same again.

Yves.

messages.subject: RE: effect of demographic variables on chi-square fit
messages.subject_clean: effect of demographic variables on chi-square fit
messages.body_plain:
Jason—

     I think that your interpretation is off the mark.  You add a variable to the model and DF goes from 3 to 7.  This means that there are 4 additional constraints in the model now, 4 additional parameters which are constrained to values that are not consistent with the data.  It is these constraints that are causing the worsening of chi-square fit.

     Take a look at your modification indices to see where this stress is being felt.  Perhaps these are unexpected constraints, or a syntax error—or maybe they are intentional and motivated by prior knowledge.  The worsening of fit does not mean that the new variables “is not needed.”  If anything, it means that the new variable has more roles to play than you are allowing.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Dear all, please allow me to show some information. This is the model

   Model1 <- '

        A=~ x1 + x2

        B =~   x3 + x4

        Y ~     A + B

        '

     I use this command: fit.m <- lavaan::sem(m, ordered=c(x1, x2, x3, x4), data= d )

This is the fit:

  Estimator                                       DWLS      Robust

  Minimum Function Test Statistic                0.222       0.736

  Degrees of freedom                                 3           3

  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.974       0.865

  Scaling correction factor                                  0.558

  Shift parameter                                            0.339

If I add the gender as a predictor of Y and then the fit gets worse

   Model2 <- '

        A=~ x1 + x2

        B =~   x3 + x4

        Y ~     A + B + Gender

        '

  Number of observations                          2527

  Estimator                                       DWLS      Robust
  Minimum Function Test Statistic               52.089      56.966
  Degrees of freedom                                 7           7
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000       0.000
  Scaling correction factor                                  0.933
  Shift parameter                                            1.155
    for simple second-order correction (Mplus variant)

The modification indices are very small. This is strange because the increase of the chi-square cannot be justified if the modification indices are so small.

Owever, if I add the gender as a predictor of one of the two latent factors as well, then the model data fit becomes excellent again:

   Model3 <- '

        A=~ x1 + x2

        B =~   x3 + x4

        Y ~     A + B + Gender

       A ~~ B

      B ~ Gender

        '

  Number of observations                          2527

  Estimator                                       DWLS      Robust
  Minimum Function Test Statistic                2.401       4.079
  Degrees of freedom                                 6           6
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.879       0.666
  Scaling correction factor                                  0.727
  Shift parameter                                            0.775

So, one question is: shouldn’t the modification idices tell me that Gender should be related to one of the latent factors? Also, does Model 3 imply the Gender affects Y directly, but also indirectly through “B ~ Gender”

Thank you for your time

messages.subject_clean: Latent variable -> manifest variable => significance indices disappear?
messages.body_plain:
Ellen—

     Probably, the model you specified is not statistically identified.  When identification fails (among other consequences), standard errors cannot be computed, and within standard errors, there is no way to assess “significance.”  If you will share your model syntax, I’m sure someone can spot the issue.

     You say that you changed a latent variable into a manifest variable.  How did you do that?  Common factors and observed variables are quite distinct.

     I agree that your sample size (200 < n < 300) is low for a model with at least 3 x 15 = 45 indicators.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject_clean: using composite of dummies instead of dummies as predictor: huge difference?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have data collected at 18 different plots. I have created 17 dummy (0/1) variables to reflect this (F2,F3,...,F18).
In the model below, the y variables are continuous and the x variables are also dummy variables, representing another categorical exogenous variable.

model1 <- '
    # regressions
        y1 + y2 + y3 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + F2 + F3 + F4 + F5 + F6 + F7 + F8 + F9 + F10 + F11 + F12 + F13 + F14 + F15 + F16 + F17 + F18
        y4 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + F2 + F3 + F4 + F5 + F6 + F7 + F8 + F9 + F10 + F11 + F12 + F13 + F14 + F15 + F16 + F17 + F18
        '
This model has a good fit (ML: 2.2, df: 3,P-value: 0.53)

I then tried this:

model2 <- '
    # composite
        plot <~ 1*F2 + F3 + F4 + F5 + F6 + F7 + F8 + F9 + F10 + F11 + F12 + F13 + F14 + F15 + F16 + F17 + F18
    # regressions
        y1 + y2 + y3 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot
        y4 ~ y1 + y2 + y3 + x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + plot
        '
Now this model has a very poor fit (ML: 306.3, df: 51, P-value: 0.000), which surprised me a little.

I noticed that in model1, certain F variables have strong effects on some y variables but not at all on others. Could this be the reason for this discrepancy?
Furthermore, which model is generally preferable?

Thank you,

M.

messages.subject_clean: spatially explicit Structural Equation Models
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

I am just writing to ask if any you know of any spatially explicit SEM examples (i.e. SEM that can deal spatial autocorrelation) implemented with lavaan? Apologies for the vague request, but I have already investigated this topic quite a bit and I have discovered for myself that there are many ways of addressing the spatial autocorrelation problem. I have some gridded data so, my spatial variables are in the format of coordinates and I have come to the conclusion that any approaches proposed for areal data would be unsuitable. I have read that one way of dealing with spatial autocorrelation is to use latent variables or to use a spatial weights matrix. The paper of reference where I have found this is: "Folmer, Henk, and Johan Oud. "How to get rid of W: a latent variables approach to modelling spatially lagged variables. Environment and planning. A 40.10 (2008): 2526". I was wondering whether there is a lavaan implementation of this? Or in general, are there any references that you recommend does anyone have some code snippets?

thanks in advance for your help,

Simone

messages.body_plain:
M—

      I think you are correct.  The first approach allows the weight for each dummy to vary across the outcome y variables, while the second imposes a proportionality constraint—the weights for each F must conform to the same proportionality relationship across at least y1 – y3.  In addition, the second syntax effectively defines plot as both (a) a composite sum of dummies and (b) a common factor with y1, y2 and y3 as indicators.  If there is no reason to expect y1, y2 and y3 to serve as three indicators of the same common factor, then there is no good reason to favor the second approach, I think.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Edward,

What you say under a) is what I was thinking.
The point you raise under b) is something I have been wondering about as well.

Is there actually any difference between specifying "y1 ~plot" or "plot =~ y1", when plot is composite or latent? You seem to suggest there isn't, right?

In textbooks I often see composites being used to sum the effects of levels of categorical variables (dummies). But then often the regressions are constructed between the composite and other latents (even with a single indicator), so no arrows directly from the composite to observed variables. Your comment b) could be the reason why.

In my model it would be difficult to only have regressions between latent variables, because of the fact that the x variables are also dummies, and I'm not sure if it makes sense to have a latent that has a single dummy variable as indicator. If not, then my model would have direct effects of these dummy x variables on the latents (again effectively making the latents into composites)...

M.

messages.subject: Re: multiple group SEM with dummy variables that are zero for certain groups
messages.subject_clean: multiple group SEM with dummy variables that are zero for certain groups
messages.body_plain:
> I have 18 "plots" each with only 5 data points... So this then would become a 18-group analysis, with not enough data per plot for a meaningful analysis.

Indeed, the small sample size would be a problem.  With so many plots, I would be inclined to approach this with a multilevel model (18*5 = 90 observations nested with 18 plots), even though 18 is on the smallish side for a Level-2 sample size.  But you are modeling more than one outcome, so you would have to run a multivariate multilevel model.  Regressing 4 outcomes (y1-y4) on x1-x4 in the first step, you would then have 18*5*4 = 360 observations, and you would distinguish effects of x1-4 on the four different outcomes with liberal use of dummy codes, as described in Ch 16 of Snijders & Bosker (2012)

http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~snijders/publ.htm#mlbook

Of course, you then have y5 and y6 regressed on y1-y4, and then y6 on y5.  If you are interested in testing indirect paths, it is certainly preferable to do so in a single model using path analysis, but you can still do so with regression and multilevel models.  You can find helpful links to reading material, macros, and online calculators on Kris Preacher's web page:

http://quantpsy.org/medn.htm

> Another thought that crossed my mind was to just get residuals per plot a priori, and then go ahead and run the SEM on these residuals. Maybe a bit crude, but then at least the variation among plots is taken care of?
>

I don't know about taken care of -- these residuals would just be mean-centering within plot?  That just sets the mean of each plot to zero, which I suppose is not a problem if you aren't looking for differences across plots.  But you wouldn't be able to compare groups 1 and 2 either, if that is something you are interested in.

Terry

Hi Ellen,

Do you still get an error if you use the "sem" function instead of the "lavaan" function?  The lavaan function has several useful defaults turned off -- it is the most flexible function, but the price of flexibility is that each parameter must be specified in your syntax OR you need to change certain defaults in lavaan() so that it behaves more like sem().  In your syntax, I notice there are latent variables with single indicators (e.g., T1V12OCCUPEXP =~ 1*T1OCCUPEXP).  You are fixing the loading to 1, but nowhere in your script do you fix the residual variance of T1OCCUPEXP to zero, which is also necessary for identification.  You can fix this either by (a) adding the appropriate parameters to the script, (b) including the argument "auto.var = TRUE" in your call to lavaan(), or perhaps most simply (c) use the sem() function instead.

I didn't study your script carefully because it is quite large :-) so I'm not sure whether there are other problems, but I would expect this to be one reason you can't get SEs.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: How does Lavaan deal with standarize coefficients?
messages.subject_clean: How does Lavaan deal with standarize coefficients?
messages.body_plain:
lavaan standardizes in the sense that the variances of observed and/or latent variables are rescaled to 1.  For anyone else interested in this topic, the article mentioned by the original poster can be downloaded here:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1890/0012-9623(2005)86[283:ITRFMR]2.0.CO;2 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1890/0012-9623(2005)86%5B283:ITRFMR%5D2.0.CO;2>

This article deals with path analysis only, not latent variable models.  Latent variables have arbitrary scales anyway, so interpreting standardized factor loadings is simply asking "how strongly correlated is this indicator with the construct it measures?", and even latent regression slopes are arbitrary because what is a 1-unit change in a variable without measurable units?  Standardized paths are just a way to ask how large the effect is, knowing it can't exceed +/- 1, although perhaps the arguments against interpreting "explained variance" in a latent variable might still apply if there is range-restriction in the indicators.

But in path analysis and multiple regression, I agree with Grace & Bollen (and several others in a long history of literature) about the limitations of interpreting "standardized" coefficients.  Although their particular suggestion is interesting (and can be calculated by a lavaan user from model results), it is by no means the only possible rescaling solution.  Andrew Gelman suggested dividing continuous predictors by 2 SDs instead of one because in most cases, that will give them roughly the same SD as binary indicators.

http://andrewgelman.com/2006/06/21/standardizing_r/

It's just another arbitrary rescaling to allow potentially less misguided comparison of different effects in the same model.  I'm not a fan of rescaling variables in any way that is not meaningful (i.e., I only want to ask how much Y changes as X changes by some amount), but when dealing with latent variables with arbitrarily set scales, I don't think we have that option.  Even using marker variables or effects-coding to identify a latent construct does not actually put the scale of a latent variable on the scale of the item (or average across items), but on the scale of the common variance in that item (e.g., see http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.7.2.210 <http://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/1082-989X.7.2.210>).

So long story short, although this is an important point to keep in mind when running path analyses in lavaan and interpreting coefficients, I don't see why Grace & Bollen's method in particular should be implemented as a preferred standardized solution in lavaan.  If syntax could be written general enough to apply to several examples, perhaps someone could make it an addition to the semTools package.

Terry

Dear Lavaan Users,

I am running a simulation study that compares Bayesian methods with traditional CFA, modeling ordinal data. For some of the simulation scenarios, I keep running into convergence issues with lavaan cfa function. I followed the lavaan categorical data tutorial on the web (http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html) and declared the items as "ordered." As an example, one of the scenarios has sample size 200, 3 items and each item with 7 response categories. I used the "WLSMV" estimator with standardization constraint. I understand that with 7 response categories, I can probably use the "ML" estimator. But I would like to see how lavaan cfa handles ordinal data, without the normal assumption.

I am relatively new to ordinal data modeling so maybe there are things that I didn't consider. If anyone has experience modeling ordinal data with lavaan cfa, I am interested in your insights.

Kind Regards,
Lily

messages.subject_clean: Calculating model likelihood for new data
messages.body_plain:
This is a great idea. I made an example below. Be careful that fit indices of the validated sample are calculated from df of the model (all parameters are fixed).

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939[HolzingerSwineford1939$school == "Pasteur",])
fitpt <- partable(fit)
fitpt$ustart[fitpt$free != 0] <- coef(fit)
fitpt$free <- 0L
fitpt$unco <- 0L

fit2 <- lavaan(fitpt, data=HolzingerSwineford1939[HolzingerSwineford1939$school == "Grant-White",], control = list(optim.method="none", optim.force.converged=TRUE))
summary(fit2)

I may make this function in semTools. Are there any papers discussed on this idea?

messages.subject: Re: How would you get fit measures for the mediation example?
messages.subject_clean: How would you get fit measures for the mediation example?
messages.body_plain:
When you do not fix any parameters in the model (i.e., estimating both direct and indirect effects), the model-implied covariance matrix is the same as observed covariance matrix. That is, your model fits perfectly--that is why chisq = 0. However, it does not mean that your model is correct. It just says that your model is one of the possible models explaining the relationships behind variables.

messages.body_plain:
I am not sure about the problems behind low convergent rates. It could be the coding errors or other issues. If the codes are correct, I would try to provide starting values. That is, we can calculate the polychoric correlations (e.g., by the psych package) and get the parameter estimates of the three-indicator model easily. If the starting values are provided, the convergent rate should increase.

Another way to check you codes is to run a model with a huge sample size. Then, check whether the convergence rates increased. Also, check the averaged parameter estimates. It should help you a lot.
